summary:
I've spent the last few weeks on a Foundry VTT module for The Long Rest, my D&D campaign manager. The app builds a session package of NPCs, reveals and encounter monsters, and the module imports it into the table's world. The rule that shaped the design is that Foundry sends GM-only documents to every player's browser. Hidden NPCs therefore never leave the app, and an NPC's numbers can cross while its prose can't. Testing ran against a real Foundry server in short windows. One run turned up a bug where Foundry strips undefined fields from the objects you pass to a create call, so the module was reading its own inputs after they'd been mutated. That bug was why the reveal poller kept stalling. The module is public now, and I've shipped several releases since.

Around that, I've been building the NPC side of The Long Rest. A DM can now link characters with relationships (leads, serves, parent, rival) and see them as an org chart and a family tree. Links are DM-only by default, and a player sees one only if it's shared and both ends are visible to them. There's also a stat-block builder that mixes parts from the SRD bestiary, with per-part attribution. While doing that I found a leak. Marked DM-only text in NPC backstories was reaching players, and so was the search index behind the Oracle, so I changed the redaction to deny by default.

The scariest find was a campaign endpoint that was returning whole database rows to any member. That meant encrypted provider keys and everyone's email address. It's now a select-only view, with emails shown to DMs only. In the same pass I found the public database API serving tables to anyone holding the anon key. I turned that off and added a migration that revokes access and enables row-level security everywhere. A later outage looked like a code problem and turned out to be the database's disk IO budget running out.

On the hardware side, I tracked down a P100 fan that seemed to blink on and off every couple of seconds. A four-hertz log showed the P100's fan holding steady. The culprit was the neighbouring GPU, whose zero-RPM mode kept toggling right at its start threshold. I also fixed the Hermes tooling that silently lost its sessions on every restart. The MCP servers were stateful by default, and making them stateless means a restart no longer breaks the client.

highlights.oneLiner: Tracked a blinking P100 fan to the neighbouring GPU's zero-RPM mode.
Made its MCP servers stateless so restarts stop dropping sessions.
Stateless by default now; a restart no longer breaks the client.
